The lexical note correctly identifies approval, but does not justify the stronger main wording.","suggested_revision":"Replace with “who approved of the teaching of Epicurus” or “who was pleased with Epicurus’s teaching.” Submit the revised wording for fresh review.","severity":"minor"}]},{"reference":"4.7","verdict":"revise","checks":{"complete_coverage":false,"no_added_claims":true,"names_and_negations":true,"lexical_fidelity":false,"uncertainties_disclosed":false},"findings":[{"source_quote":"πολὺν ἐποιούμην λόγον, ὅτι ἀνὴρ πρὸς γένους Τιβερίου Καίσαρος ὢν καὶ πάσης ἑλληνικῆς παιδείας ἐξησκημένος ὑπὸ βαρβάρου τινός, τὴν προσηγορίαν Πέτρου, τὰ Ἰουδαίων ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν ἠπάτηται.","english_quote":"I have told you at length. Although he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar and has been trained in every branch of Greek education, he has been deceived by a certain barbarian named Peter into doing and saying the things of the Jews.","issue":"The substantive clauses survive, and a concessive interpretation of the participles is defensible. However, the sentence break leaves ὅτι’s reporting or explanatory connection to the preceding account unrepresented. “Although” can express the participles’ concession, but does not itself represent ὅτι. The notes do not address the content-versus-causal attachment.","suggested_revision":"Explicitly connect the account to the following clause, for example: “I have spoken to you at length, telling you that, although he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar and has been trained in every branch of Greek education, he has been deceived …” Note that ὅτι can alternatively introduce the reason for Appion’s extended discussion, “because …,” and explain the chosen attachment.
